newsitem.title: USA: Residents take cover as hurricane heads for U.S..
newsitem.headline: Residents take cover as hurricane heads for U.S..

text.p: Hurricane Fran headed for the southeastern United States coast on Thursday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people living in North and South Carolina to seek refuge inland from the dangerous storm.

The National Hurricane Center predicted Fran's most likely target would be the coastline between 300-year-old Charleston, a city battered seven years ago by deadly Hurricane Hugo, and the state's resort area Myrtle Beach.
"At this time Hurricane Fran is about as large as Hurricane Hugo and has the potential to become just as strong," the Miami-based center said.
Hugo ravaged Charleston on Sept. 21, 1989, with winds of more than 140 mph (225 kph). That hurricane was blamed for 27 deaths, it destroyed 17,000 homes and caused more than $7 billion in damage.
Hurricane warnings for Fran stretched across the coastline of four states early on Thursday, from Georgia, through to the Carolinas and Virginia.

At 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), the center of Fran was about 260 miles (420 km) southeast of Charleston and was moving north-northwest. The center of the hurricane was expected to hit land -- either North or South Carolina -- late on Thursday or early Friday morning.
Fran's wicked winds reached 115 mph (185 kmh) overnight and forecasters said the hurricane could strengthen over the next 24 hours.
Emergency officials enforced mandatory evacuations of beachfront properties in South Carolina. Officials knocked on resident's doors to move out any stragglers wanting to stay.
Nursing homes took the elderly to shelters or called relatives to collect them and emergency teams worked overnight to pull down roadside billboards.

"The storm has moved a little bit more north of Charleston but we could start experiencing some effects, namely rain and winds, by about 8 a.m. (1200 GMT) or 9 a.m. (1300 GMT)," said Cathy Haynes, deputy director of the Emergency Preparedness Department for Charleston County.
She said more than a dozen schools had been turned into shelters in the area.
Coastal roads from Georgia to North Carolina were clogged on Wednesday when residents, visitors, and sun worshipers taking in the last bit of summer at the beach had to flee.

Bumper-to-bumper traffic streamed out of Charleston, a preserved city of antebellum plantations, stunning gardens, open markets, and host of the famous Spoleto Festival U.S.A, a comprehensive arts festival.
Residents and merchants locked shutters over windows, taped some, and mounted plywood on others in preparation of the gale-force winds due to begin lashing the coast on Thursday.
"The people of Charleston learned a lot from Hugo," said Charleston Mayor Joe Riley.
South Carolina Gov. David Beasley declared a statewide state of emergency early on Wednesday and called for evacuation of beachfront property and low-lying areas in six counties.
Georgia Gov. Zell Miller declared a state of emergency in 11 counties along the coast and urged voluntary evacuations. It was mandatory for those on barrier islands.
Further north, emergency management officials worried about the dangerous strength of Fran, evacuated residents of Ocracoke Island, North Carolina.

Peter Stone, emergency management manager for the island that dots North Carolina's famed Outer Banks, said the decision was based on the proximity and strength of the storm. "It was time to get everybody the hell out of here," he said.

At Cape Canaveral, about halfway up the Florida coast, NASA rolled the space shuttle Atlantis back to its massive garage as a precaution against storm conditions, delaying its takeoff. Atlantis, already six weeks late, had been due to blast off on Sept. 14 on a mission to pick up U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid from the Russian Mir space station and drop off her replacement, John Blaha.
